To extol someone or something means to praise it very enthusiastically and in a big way — to speak or write about it with great admiration, making it sound wonderful, impressive, or excellent.

It is not just a quiet "well done." It is loud, strong, glowing praise. When you extol something, you are lifting it up with your words.

She extolled her doctor's kindness to everyone she met.

This means she went around telling people how wonderfully kind her doctor was — enthusiastically and with great admiration.

Many words mean "to praise," but extol carries a specific energy. It suggests:

1. The praise is intense and enthusiastic, not mild or polite.
Saying "he's pretty good" is not extolling. Saying "he is absolutely brilliant, talented beyond measure, and everyone should know it" — that is extolling.

2. The praise is usually expressed out loud or in writing — to other people. Extolling is a public, outward act. You are not just privately admiring something; you are telling others how great it is.

3. The praise is sincere, not sarcastic. Extolling always carries genuine admiration. You cannot extol something ironically (unlike "praising" which can sometimes be used sarcastically).
How It Is Used in Sentences

The most classic pattern is:

extol + the + [quality/virtue/benefit] + of + [someone/something]

Examples:

  • The coach constantly extolled the virtues of hard work and discipline.

(= The coach enthusiastically and repeatedly praised hard work and discipline as being wonderful.)

  • Doctors extol the benefits of walking at least 30 minutes a day.

(= Doctors speak very highly of this habit and encourage everyone to follow it.)

  • The travel writer extolled the beauty of the small Italian village.

(= The writer praised the village's beauty in a glowing, enthusiastic way in their writing.)

  • He extolled his mentor's wisdom at every opportunity.

(= He took every chance to tell people how incredibly wise his mentor was.)

You can also simply extol a person directly:

  • The whole team extolled their captain after the championship win.
The Most Common Phrase: "Extol the Virtues of..."

By far the most common way you will see this word used is in the phrase "extol the virtues of" something. This means to enthusiastically tell others about all the great qualities and benefits of something.

  • My grandmother always extolled the virtues of waking up early.
  • The advertisement extolled the virtues of their new skincare product.

When you see this phrase, it can sometimes carry a very slight hint that the speaker is perhaps overdoing it a little — being a bit too enthusiastic, as if trying to convince others. But this is subtle, and the word itself is not negative.
The Tone and Register of the Word

Extol is a formal or semi-formal word. You will mostly see it in:

  • Written articles, books, and reviews
  • Speeches and presentations
  • News reports
  • Literary writing

You would not normally say it in casual everyday conversation. You wouldn't text a friend: "I extol this pizza place." Instead, in casual speech, people say things like "rave about," "can't stop talking about," or "go on and on about."

But in writing, or in any slightly formal context, "extol" fits perfectly and sounds sophisticated.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Since you may encounter similar words, here is how extol stands apart:

  • Praise — This is the broad, general word. You can praise anything, mildly or strongly. Extol is a more intense, elevated version of praise.
  • Compliment — A compliment is usually a single, specific nice thing you say to someone directly (e.g., "Your hair looks great"). Extolling is broader and more enthusiastic than a compliment.
  • Commend — To commend is to formally recommend or approve of something, often in an official context (e.g., a manager commending an employee). It is more measured and less emotionally charged than extolling.
  • Laud — Very close in meaning to extol. Also means to praise highly. Laud is slightly more formal and less commonly used. If you know extol, you essentially know laud too.
  • Glorify — To glorify means to make something seem more wonderful or heroic than it perhaps really is — it can sometimes have a negative implication (like glorifying violence). Extol does not carry that negative implication.

• It does not mean to silently admire something. The praise must be expressed outwardly.
  • It does not mean to exaggerate dishonestly — it is genuine, heartfelt praise.
  • It is not a casual, mild word. If the praise is small or ordinary, "extol" is too strong a word for it.

When you extol something, you sing its praises so loudly and enthusiastically that everyone around you hears how wonderful you think it is.
